look_here_first: TEXAS WILD-RICE — ENDANGERED: from a permitted riverbank viewpoint, look for long ribbonlike submerged leaves streaming with the current in the upper San Marcos River. When flowering panicles emerge, LOWER spreading branches carry drooping, awnless male spikelets; UPPER ascending branches carry narrow female spikelets with one ~10–20 mm lemma awn. Ordinary glumes are absent/obscure. Giant cutgrass instead arranges sexes along the SAME branch. Never touch, collect, trample, transplant or enter protected stands. Without visible flowering anatomy, keep the identification provisional.

measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.status: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS — reference-measured field key, no-contact endangered-species protocol
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.growth_form: Submerged aquatic perennial, with rooted stolons and ribbonlike underwater leaves; USFWS describes clonal growth. GrassBase's morphology paragraph labels the plant annual even though its Kew overview and USFWS call it perennial; preserve that source conflict rather than changing canonical biology.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.ligule_collar: Published GrassBase: eciliate MEMBRANOUS ligule 5–15 mm; blades 10–40 mm wide. These dimensions are source measurements, not demonstrated in the three stored photos. Do not manipulate endangered plants to expose a collar.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.flowering_architecture: Open panicle about 20–30 cm long; lower spreading branches with staminate (male) spikelets and upper ascending branches with pistillate (female) spikelets. Confirm branch origin in an intact image before placing sex-specific arrows.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.male_spikelet: Male spikelets linear 7–9 mm, awnless; male lemma five-veined. Yellow dangling anthers are male flower parts, not glumes or female awns.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.female_spikelet: Female spikelets narrow, about 10 mm and one-flowered; female lemma about 10 mm, three-veined, bearing one 10–20 mm awn (GrassBase). The 1986 species study reports 10–25 mm female awns; preserve range difference.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.glumes: Ordinary paired glumes ABSENT or obscure in both sexes; do not arrow nonexistent glumes or mistake lemma/palea for glumes.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.awn: The female lemma bears a single terminal awn, whereas male spikelets lack awns. Distinguish this structure from exposed anthers.
measured_diagnostic_key_20261023.local_lookalikes: Zizaniopsis miliacea (giant cutgrass): large emergent marsh grass, male and female spikelets on different positions along the SAME panicle branch, versus Zizania's lower male and upper female BRANCHES. Leersia oryzoides (rice cutgrass): rough-bladed wetland grass with flattened one-flowered spikelets, but not the same sex-separated flowering arrangement. Habitat or ribbonlike leaves alone cannot certify Z. texana.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — STREAMING RIBBON LEAVES
field_id_short_tiles.short: Protected aquatic perennial: long submerged ribbons flowing with the river current.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Observe only from a permitted vantage: long, flat submerged leaves stream downstream and flowering shoots may emerge. Similar aquatic grasses occur nearby; the source-verified habitat and actual flowers matter. USFWS describes clonal rooted stolons. Never handle, enter stands, pull, collect, or disturb this federally/state endangered plant.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · TRUE COLLAR — A DOCUMENTED PHOTO GAP
field_id_short_tiles.short: Published membranous ligule 5–15 mm; root growth perennial; collar unverified in gallery.
field_id_short_tiles.details: GrassBase reports a true, non-hair-fringed membranous ligule approximately 5–15 mm. TPWD describes leaves commonly 3–25 mm wide; broader treatments differ. These are published ranges, not measurements from current JPEGs. Do not part a leaf or expose roots on a protected wild specimen just to see a ligule. An authorized cultivated research specimen may supply this close-up.
field_id_short_tiles.status: REFERENCE MEASUREMENTS ONLY — NONCONTACT PHOTO HOLD

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · MALE LOWER / FEMALE UPPER BRANCHES
field_id_short_tiles.short: Panicle ~20–30 cm: spreading lower male branches; ascending upper female branches.
field_id_short_tiles.details: The 1986 botanical study describes staminate spikelets on lower spreading panicle branches and pistillate spikelets on upper ascending branches. Existing panels show exposed male anthers but do not independently resolve the whole sex-position map on one intact panicle. Identify anthers, stigmas or awns before placing sex-specific arrows; do not infer sex from an isolated crop.
field_id_short_tiles.status: MALE ANTHERS VISIBLE — FULL PANICLE MAP MISSING

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · MALE SPIKELET — AWNLESS, GLUMES ABSENT
field_id_short_tiles.short: Male spikelets ~7–9 mm; five-veined lemma; no long awn.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Published male spikelets are linear, approximately 7–9 mm long, awnless, with a five-veined lemma. Ordinary paired glumes are absent: do not label a lemma, palea or anther as a glume. Existing Joey Santore and USFWS panels visibly show dangling anthers, but do not establish a measured male spikelet or count its lemma veins. Use only safe no-contact or authorized ex situ imagery.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · FEMALE SPIKELET — ONE TERMINAL LEMMA AWN
field_id_short_tiles.short: Female spikelet ~10 mm; 3-veined lemma; one 10–20(–25) mm awn.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Published female spikelets are approximately 10 mm long with a roughly 10 mm three-veined lemma bearing one terminal awn. GrassBase reports ~10–20 mm; Vaughan (1986) reports ~10–25 mm. Preserve this source difference. Glumes are absent in female spikelets too. No existing gallery panel proves the actual female awn insertion at a calibrated scale. Do not collect or dissect wild protected plants.
field_id_short_tiles.status: PUBLISHED ANATOMY — FEMALE AWN PHOTO HOLD

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · LOOK-ALIKES AND PUBLIC-READY GATE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Compare giant cutgrass and rice cutgrass; remain FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS.
field_id_short_tiles.details: Giant cutgrass (Zizaniopsis miliacea) is a large emergent reedlike marsh grass; rice cutgrass (Leersia oryzoides) has rough leaf margins and different spikelet anatomy. Do not rely solely on plume shape or oversimplify disputed Zizaniopsis male/female branch placement. NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO: no-contact full flowering panicle showing sexed branch origins, naturally visible female awn, and an already-exposed collar if possible; otherwise use authorized ex situ material. NEEDS_SITE_QA: verify eight archived photos, three Joey CC BY-NC rights records, five USFWS public-domain credits, eight existing arrows and public/mobile rendering. No handling, collection, wading into protected stands or unpermitted disturbance.
